description: Soñamos mas de lo que dormimos
summary:
CardioMe is an autonomous onboard cardiac monitoring and triage system designed for deep-space missions. In microgravity, 55% of evaluated crew members have developed stagnant or reversed internal jugular vein flow, yet reviewing a long electrocardiogram today takes hours or days while waiting for a downlink window and a specialist on Earth. On a mission to Mars, with round-trip communication delays reaching 44 minutes, an astronaut's heart cannot wait.

Our solution pairs a reusable single-lead biometric chest patch with offline software that analyzes cardiac signals in seconds. Its Python causal analysis engine—built on 51 nodes and 104 relationships from NASA's Human System Risk Board—combines ECG metrics with radiation exposure, fluid shifts, and real-time cabin variables. Built with Flutter, FastAPI, and PostgreSQL using a Store-and-Forward queue, CardioMe identifies the probable cause, coordinates step-by-step crew response and resource staging onboard, and compresses ground transmissions from ~43 MB per day to a few kilobytes per high-priority event.
details:
During long-duration spaceflight, 55% of evaluated crew members (6 of 11) develop stagnant or reversed blood flow in the internal jugular vein around flight day 50. Despite this risk, reviewing a long electrocardiogram today takes hours or days because the file is stored onboard, waits for a downlink window to Earth, and requires reading by a specialist. On a mission to Mars, where the signal takes up to 22 minutes each way (44 minutes round trip), that waiting time is unviable during a medical emergency. CardioMe solves this bottleneck through an autonomous medical node that monitors the heart and coordinates the crew in seconds without an internet connection. The astronaut wears a 120 x 40 mm adhesive biometric patch on the chest with a maximum thickness of 8 mm that records a single-lead electrocardiogram at 250 Hz day and night. To avoid the pressure of full vests and the motion noise of wristwatches, the patch adheres directly to the chest with two electrodes separated by 80 mm, using a reusable central electronic module (35 x 25 mm) where only the skin adhesive layer is replaced.

The signal travels via Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) to the onboard software, where heart rate, beat-to-beat irregularity (R-R), and contact quality are evaluated against the crew member's physiological limits. Rather than analyzing the heart in isolation or displaying clinical screens meant for cardiologists on Earth, we designed an operational tool for the astronauts themselves to act immediately. The system cross-references vital signs with the cabin's environmental status, sleep hours, radiation, fluid shifts, and clotting risk. This way, it distinguishes whether tachycardia comes from a primary arrhythmia or from carbon dioxide retention in the spacesuit or sleeping quarters. When one or several crew members enter a red alert at the same time, CardioMe first identifies if there is a shared environmental cause, assigns which healthy crewmate should assist each patient, and indicates which resources to prepare—such as the 12-lead monitor, oxygen supply, or air purge—through a step-by-step care plan while the response from Earth arrives. All system rules are transparent and always explain the clinical reason behind every alert.

To build the prototype, we developed an interactive interface in Flutter (Dart) with simulated data and programmed a causal analysis engine in Python and NumPy that models a Bayesian network with 51 nodes and 104 medical relationships. These links come from NASA's Human System Risk Board causal graphs on cardiovascular adaptations and venous thromboembolism (NASA NTRS 20220016588), complemented by radiation monitoring studies from the Canadian Space Agency (CSA). The backend architecture uses FastAPI and PostgreSQL with a Store-and-Forward transmission queue that stores normal activity on the spacecraft and reduces transmission to Earth from about 43 MB of raw electrocardiogram per day to a few kilobytes per priority event. During development, we used Claude (Anthropic) and Gemini (Google) to support system design, programming in Flutter and Python, visual generation of the patch, and slide drafting, reviewing and testing every component as a team. This medical autonomy protects crews heading to the Moon or Mars and offers a triage workflow applicable in rural communities on Earth where there are no nearby cardiologists either.
